To disburse means to pay out money from a fund, account, or organized source — to the people or places it is meant for.

The key word here is "pay out." When someone disburses money, they are releasing it from where it was being held and sending it to whoever is supposed to receive it.
The Central Idea Behind the Word

Think of it this way. Imagine a charity collects donations throughout the year and keeps all that money in a fund. Then, at the end of the year, it sends that money out to the hospitals, schools, and communities it supports. That act of sending the money out to its intended destinations — that is disbursing.

The word almost always implies three things:

The money was held somewhere first — in a bank account, a fund, a loan, a government treasury, or an organizational budget. Then, there is a specific reason or plan for the payment — it is not random; it goes to particular people or purposes. And finally, it is usually an institution, organization, official body, or an authorized person doing it, not just anyone spending their own cash.

This is important, because "pay" and "spend" are the words you likely already know, and they feel similar.

"Spend" is what you do with your own money when you buy something. "Pay" is general — you pay a shopkeeper, you pay a friend back for lunch. These words are casual and everyday.

"Disburse" is more formal and specific. It is almost never used for personal, everyday transactions. You would not say "I disbursed money for pizza." Instead, it is used when an organization, government, bank, or institution is systematically releasing funds according to a plan, obligation, or approved process. It carries a sense of official responsibility and organized distribution.
Where You Will See This Word

Loans and banking: When a bank approves your home loan or student loan, it does not just hand you a bag of cash immediately. It disburses the loan — meaning it officially releases and transfers the loan amount to you (or directly to the seller or college) on the scheduled date.

Government and aid: Governments disburse welfare payments to eligible citizens. International organizations like the World Bank or IMF disburse funds to countries for development or economic recovery.

Grants and scholarships: A university disburses scholarship money to students at the start of each semester. A foundation disburses grants to researchers whose projects it has approved.

Nonprofits and NGOs: An aid organization receives donations and later disburses those funds to disaster-affected communities.

Legal and financial settings: A lawyer might disburse a client's settlement amount. A company's finance department disburses salaries to employees.

In real life, you will most often see "disburse" paired with words like:

disburse funds, disburse payments, disburse a loan, disburse aid, disburse grants, disburse money.

"The bank will disburse the loan amount directly into your account within three business days of signing the agreement."

"The government disbursed emergency relief funds to the flood-affected regions within a week."

"The nonprofit organization has disbursed over two million dollars in grants to community health programs this year."

"The World Bank announced that it will disburse $800 million to support education reforms in developing nations."

"After the insurance claim was verified and approved, the company disbursed the full settlement to the policyholder."

"The project manager is authorized to disburse up to $15,000 for approved operational expenses."

When you come across this word in its noun form, you will see two versions: disbursement and disbursal. Both mean the same thing — the act of disbursing, or a specific amount of money that was paid out. "Disbursement" is more commonly used in formal and financial writing.

For example: "The disbursement of scholarship funds will take place at the beginning of March."

Or: "The organization tracked every disbursement carefully to ensure transparency."

Many learners mix up disburse and disperse. These look nearly identical, but they mean entirely different things.

Disburse = pay out money.
Disperse = scatter or spread out (people, objects, particles, crowds, etc.).

A police officer disperses a crowd. A bank disburses a loan. Never swap them.

To disburse is to officially pay out money — from a fund, account, treasury, or organized source — to the people or purposes it is designated for. It is a formal word used in banking, finance, government, law, and charitable work. It is not used for personal, everyday spending. The noun form is disbursement. And it has nothing to do with the word "disperse."
